method: A matched resistive pad trades loss for a stable impedance. The voltage ratio is K = 10^(dB/20). A pi pad is one series arm between two shunt arms: the series arm is Z0 times (K squared minus one) divided by twice K, and each shunt arm is Z0 times (K plus one) divided by (K minus one). A T pad is one shunt arm between two series arms: each series arm is Z0 times (K minus one) divided by (K plus one), and the shunt arm is Z0 times twice K divided by (K squared minus one). At six decibels in fifty ohms K is 1.995262, so a pi pad needs 37.352 ohms in series and 150.476 ohms at each end, while a T pad needs 16.619 ohms in each series arm and 66.931 ohms in the shunt arm. The page also picks the nearest 1% E96 value in each decade by relative error, then recomputes the loss of that fitted combination from its chain matrix and reports the input match as a return loss, so the cost of rounding to real parts is visible before the circuit is built; a fitted build that matches poorly is reported with a low return loss rather than hidden. Attenuation is limited to 0.1 to 40 decibels and the system impedance to 5 to 1000 ohms; text, exponent notation, zero, negative values, out of range values and an unknown topology are refused with the field named. The values assume an ideal resistive network terminated in Z0 at both ports: component tolerance drift, lead inductance, stray capacitance, power dissipation and the distributed behaviour of the layout at high frequency are not modelled, and the page stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Attenuator design practice: a matched pi attenuator is a series arm between two shunt arms whose values follow from the voltage ratio K = 10^(dB/20).
Attenuator design practice: a matched T attenuator is a shunt arm between two series arms, derived from the same voltage ratio.
IEC 60063 preferred values: the E96 series is the 1% resistor grid, and the nearest value in each decade is chosen by relative error.
